C005.subject: Combinatorial generalization on out-of-distribution compositional tasks
C005.object: representations that are explicitly factorized into disjoint symbolic subspaces, one per compositional role, rather than by representations with a strict alignment to the task grammar
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Combinatorial generalization on out-of-distribution compositional tasks representations that are explicitly factorized into disjoint symbolic subspaces, one per compositional role, rather than by representations with a strict alignment to the task grammar]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiments comparing systematic generalization of neural networks with factorized vs. grammar-aligned representations on SCAN-style tasks (e.g., compositionality benchmarks from Lake & Baroni 2018, or COGS) — These benchmarks measure combinatorial generalization on out-of-distribution compositional tasks. Directly comparing factorized subspace representations (e.g., via modular networks or disentangled latent codes) against representations that strictly encode the task grammar (e.g., through syntactic attention or tree-structured RNNs) would provide concrete empirical evidence for or against the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis using the framework of algebraic compositionality and disentanglement (e.g., Higgins et al. 2018 on symmetry-based disentanglement, or Greff et al. 2020 on binding by subspaces) — A theoretical derivation of the conditions under which disjoint symbolic subspaces enable compositional generalization better than grammar-aligned representations would clarify the hypothesis. For instance, analyzing whether factorization into role-specific subspaces provably reduces interference during re-composition of unseen combinations, while strict grammar alignment may overfit to training distribution patterns.

[PATH:literature] Literature review spanning work on compositional generalization in neural networks, including meta-learning for composition (e.g., Chang et al. 2019, Keysers et al. 2020) and disentangled representation learning (e.g., Locatello et al. 2019, Montero et al. 2021) — A systematic meta-analysis of published results comparing factorized vs. grammar-aligned approaches across multiple compositional generalization benchmarks (e.g., SCAN, COGS, CFQ, gSCAN) would reveal whether the hypothesis holds consistently or is domain-dependent. This can aggregate evidence from existing studies to assess the confidence level of the hypothesis.

scope.domain: hierarchically compositional tasks with discrete roles

qualifier.temporal: during the period of controlled simulation experiments (2023-2024)

C006.object: a strict alignment between the algebraic structure of learned representations and the compositional grammar of the task, even in tasks with hierarchical composition

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiments comparing systematic generalization of neural networks on hierarchically compositional tasks (e.g., SCAN, COGS, CFQ) with and without explicit algebraic structure in latent representations — Directly tests whether alignment between representation algebra and task grammar is necessary for compositional generalization. If models with mismatched algebraic structure still generalize, the hypothesis is supported; if they fail, it is refuted.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of the relationship between compositionality and representation geometry, such as the 'disentanglement vs. compositionality' literature and results on the necessity of certain algebraic properties (e.g., commutativity, associativity) for systematic generalization — Provides formal conditions under which alignment is required. If theorems show that strict alignment is unnecessary for hierarchical composition, the hypothesis is confirmed; if they prove necessity, it is refuted.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing empirical studies on compositional generalization (e.g., from NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML 2022-2025) that report whether learned representations exhibit algebraic structure aligned with task grammar and how that correlates with out-of-distribution performance — Synthesizes broad evidence across multiple models and tasks to assess the general pattern. If most successful models lack strict alignment, the hypothesis gains support; if alignment is consistently observed, the hypothesis is weakened.
